reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper is in my opinion an outstanding contribution to ochre studies. The identification of an
ochre community of practice represents an innovative approach that certainly represents a
necessary step in the study of earth mineral pigments. The authors use different analytical
techniques, including pXRF, NAA, LA-ICP-MS, XRD and Raman spectroscopy to characterise raw
materials from different archaeological sites and potential sources. These methods are in line with
the questions raised and enable the authors to reconstruct patterns of raw material acquisition that
are of great interest to the understanding of late MSA and LSA cultures. All of the data is thoroughly
presented in the article and supplementary data. I strongly recommend publication.
Please find below a few minor comments and suggestions by page number:
Page 3
- “The analysis of earth mineral pigments, or ochres, has played a role in interpretations of cognitive
behaviors (6, 7), has become synonymous with rock art and symbolic expressions”
I would not say that the use of ochre is synonymous with symbolic expressions. As this is a quite
debated question, I would advise being more cautious in this statement.
- “Here, we apply the concept to the chaîne opératoire of ochre behaviors”.
Considering that the technological aspects of the ochre exploitation strategies and possible uses of
ochre are not explored in this paper, I would say that the concept of community of practice is
mostly applied here to raw material acquisition strategies, rather than the entire ochre chaîne
opératoire,
- “These components were selected (…) also for sociocultural reasons, such as spiritual potency
and the geographic origins of minerals. The ochre chaîne opératoire was an inherently social
activity that existed as part of a broader system of relations that had cultural significance to people
living in the MSA and LSA.”
I agree with this statement. However, we do not have direct evidence of it for MSA and LSA cultures.
I would advise moderating this section by specifying that it is a likely hypothesis.
- “Here, we show evidence for long term, regional-scale behavioral stability in ochre provisioning
and transport, but also, distinctive site-specific variations in procurement and technological
choices”
I would remove “technological choices” from this section, as the scarcity of modified ochre pieces
does not allow to discuss technological aspects related to ochre exploitation.
Page 4
- “communities of practice”
This concept sometimes appears in italics and sometimes not. Please be consistent.
- “Following the local traditional nomenclature and geology of Eswatini, we use the term ochre
to describe all earth-derived mineral pigments, with specific reference to red or yellow ochre (iron
oxide and iron-rich clay), black ochre (magnetite, manganese oxides, or charcoal) and
white ochre (kaolin)”.
I understand the authors’ choice to use traditional nomenclature of Eswatini. I consider, however,
that “black ochre” and “white ochre” are slightly confusing terms, as they do not correspond to
what is usually referred to as “ochre” in the literature. The term “ochre” is already quite ambiguous
as it is, so I would recommend avoiding its use when referring to colouring materials other than iron
oxides. In any case, I see that these terms are not used throughout the text, so this doesn’t affect
the rest of the paper.
Page 13
- Tables 1 and 2
Some of the archaeological sites do not appear on table 1 (Mlawula I and II, Nsangwini, Hlalakahle,
Mphaphati I, Ndhlozane shelter). Are there no dates for these sites?
Page 15
- In figure legend 2b, what do the authors mean exactly by “use wear”?
Page 16
- Figure 3 is missing
Page 17
- Figure 4 is missing.
Page 19-20
- Figure 5 and 6: I recommend specifying in the figure legend that the scatterplot represents the
PCA of NAA results.
Page 27-28
- Figures 8 and 9: adding the total number of iron and manganese artifacts per phase to the figure
might be useful to evaluate how significative these proportions are, and to have an idea of the
stratigraphic distribution of these pieces.
Page 32
- “Hunter-gatherers would have conducted some testing (grinding, scoring, mixing, applying to
various surfaces, see SI-Text 2.0) to understand their qualities for rock art or body paint,
adhesives, and other potential uses”.
I was surprised by the fact that the technological observations conducted on the archaeological
assemblage are only mentioned in the supplementary materials. I think that, although very few
pieces show modifications, this aspect deserves to appear in the main text, and maybe they could
be presented in the form of a table. Unless I’m mistaken, I don’t think there is detailed information
on the stratigraphic provenance of modified pieces (in addition to what appears in page 29 of the
Supplementary text). In the case of Sibebe, it is not specified in the supplementary data which
ochre typologies show anthropogenic modifications.
Page 33
“The infrequent long-distance transport of ochre could be indicative of the itinerant movement of
painters or tangoma (…) the localized activities associated with its chaîne opératoire were varied
and contextually-contingent communities of practice”.
While these ethnographic examples are of great interest and show the cultural significance of
ochre, I think that using this information to discuss MSA and LSA societies is a complex task. I
would suggest the authors mention the fact that there are debates surrounding ethnoarchaeology,
and on whether one should establish analogies between prehistoric societies and ethnographic
data. Maybe it would be interesting to cite some authors that have discussed this issue, such as
David and Kramer 2001 (David N, Kramer C. Ethnoarchaeology in Action. Cambridge: Cambridge
University Press; 2001.).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
LSA in Eswatini. The authors have sampled ochre from known archaeological sites from recent or
ancient excavations, as well as from potential ancient mining sites. A panel of physico-chemical
analyses (NAA, La-ICPMS, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, XRF) has allowed them to defined different
groups of ochre (Mn or Fe rich types) and to propose sourcing for the archaeological samples. Then
discussions about procurement strategies over time are presented.
The paper is overall well written and structured with a very complete set of data and documents. I
am not competent to judge the way in which the statistical study was carried out. I am also a bit
sceptical about the fact that part of the discussion could be derived from general considerations on
ochre use (ex: the need to share the location of sources and the way to use them) and not from
the data presented and analysed here. This should not prevent the paper to be published however. I
have only minor suggestions and comments:
- I think a summary map (or several) showing relations between archaeological sites and mining
sources deduced from the analyses would be useful. I add to draw arrows on the map in order to
follow the conclusions, so it might be good if this was already provided by the authors.
- Fig. 5b: why don’t you plot G1b there?
- Fig 6 (and SI fig24): I am confused: the % indicated for PC1 and 2 on the axes does not correspond
to the ones indicated in the caption. Was it supposed to be a “zoom” of Fig 5a for the “east” groups?
Or do you change the composition of the PC for better separation? It may help to use the same
symbols in Fig 5 and 6. Please also indicate the source corresponding to the ellipses as you do for
Fig 5b. The caption says they are known but the text suggests it is not really the case. Please
modify/explain.
- Fig 7: again maybe, label the ellipse with the corresponding source.
- Line 295: “the use of a proportionally higher number of different sources of both iron and
manganese oxides is evident”. I wonder. There are only one or two more compare to the LSA or
final LSA phases…
- Fig8 and 9: I would suggest you also add chronological indications for each phase, and you
indicate (for example with dashes or stars), which groups are “local” and which one are not.
- You indicate 20 samples for G2a, but I can count only eight on the figures.
- “but not predating the Oakhurst litho-technocomplex phase” : which one is it?
- “Subsequent experimentation would have been needed to test the extracted ochres and their
physicochemical properties”: I understand what you mean, but I find it odd to speak about testing
physicochemical properties when Stone Age experimenters did not know any thing about physics
and chemistry. Maybe another wording would be more appropriate?
- “the impurities present in most of the eastern ochre sources led to the reduced the tinting
strength of the material”-> “led to reduce”
- Concerning the OSL analysis at Lion’s Cavern: In addition to the photo (Fig. SI2), it would be
good to have a drawing of the stratigraphy with localized OSL samples. A short explanation also on the
build-up of stratigraphic sequence would be welcome, since the way in which a quarry sites is
forms might be different from the way in which any living sites builds up.
- I guess (but maybe I am wrong?) that the matrix embedding the quartz grains is unusually rich in
iron. Did you consider this in your calculations of dose rate? How different would be the
absorption coefficients?
- Lines 742-749: you do not explicitly tell which system you use for the alpha efficiency. It looks
typical of a a-value but you should say it.
- While you calculate the gamma dose rate from the U, Th, K content of the surrounding, you are not
very explicit about the process and Table 6 presents the data only for the OSL samples. How many
samples did you use to reconstruct the gamma dose? How did you deal with heterogeneities if any?
- In Table 6: I guess the K content is actually in %, not in ppm. Please also indicate that the DR
is in Gy/ka. I think the second digit is not significant for the De, nor for the Age. Please remove
them. This is also the case in Table 1 in the main text.

necessary step in the study of earth mineral pigments. The authors use different analytical

Reply: Thank you for your kind words and valuable feedback on our manuscript.
Page 3
- “The analysis of earth mineral pigments, or ochres, has played a role in interpretations of
cognitive behaviors (6, 7), has become synonymous with rock art and symbolic expressions”
I would not say that the use of ochre is synonymous with symbolic expressions. As this is a quite
debated question, I would advise being more cautious in this statement.
Reply: We changed the text to convey that ochre is “linked to” instead of “synonymous with”
rock art and symbolic expression.
- “Here, we apply the concept to the chaîne opératoire of ochre behaviors”.
Considering that the technological aspects of the ochre exploitation strategies and possible uses
of ochre are not explored in this paper, I would say that the concept of community of practice is
mostly applied here to raw material acquisition strategies, rather than the entire ochre chaîne
opératoire,
Reply: We have added some additional writing to the main text that describes what we can
currently convey with confidence about the uses of ochre. Please note that we are constrained by
the journal word count. We moved some of our discussion on ochre usewear from the
supplementary text to the main text and have added and cited a brief comparison to the
proportion of ochre usewear found at comparable sites. We also added further commentary
reiterating the use of ochre directly at the sites for rock art. Pasted below is the text we added.
Ochre Processing and Use
Figure 10 illustrates a selection of ochre samples exhibiting usewear from the Sibebe
assemblage. Remarkably, only nine of the 931 (< 1%) artifacts examined this entire study
showed clear evidence of usewear, six of which were from Sibebe, and four of those limited to
the uppermost stratum at that site. The remaining modified ochres were from Siphiso (n=2) and
Nyonyane (n=1). This low proportion of modified ochre artifacts in the Eswatini assemblages is
in contrast to the few other comparable systematic studies on ochre processing. For instance,
Hodgskiss’ analysis of MSA ochre at Sibudu (52) identified 7.57% of the total assemblage
exhibited evidence for usewear (more commonly during the pre-Still Bay period ~77kya), and
Hodgskiss and Wadley identified usewear (grinding, scoring, rubbing) in 11.2% of the
assemblage at Rose Cottage Cave (53). The results from the Eswatini assemblage suggests that
the more common method for preparing ochres for use as paint to for objects, rock walls, or as
body paint, may have been through grinding or pulverizing whole pieces using an anvil or
mortar and pestle, rather than via repeated abrasion or scoring of the ochre pieces against other
textured surfaces to produce powder.
Other indicators for the processing and end-use of ochre are evident in the abundance of
rock art. There are currently 52 documented (yet unpublished) rock art sites across Eswatini,
several of them coincident with the assemblages studied here (Nsangwini, Sibebe, Muti Muti,
Ndhlozane). The artifact assemblage recovered from Nsangwini also yielded 17 lithics (chert,
hornfels) stained with dry-rubbed ochre or spatters of prepared ochre paint. Further study of
those stone tools is currently underway.
- “These components were selected (…) also for sociocultural reasons, such as spiritual potency
and the geographic origins of minerals. The ochre chaîne opératoire was an inherently social
activity that existed as part of a broader system of relations that had cultural significance to
people living in the MSA and LSA.”
I agree with this statement. However, we do not have direct evidence of it for MSA and LSA
cultures. I would advise moderating this section by specifying that it is a likely hypothesis.
Reply: To avoid any misunderstanding, we removed use of the term “cultural” in the quoted
passage.
- “Here, we show evidence for long term, regional-scale behavioral stability in ochre
provisioning and transport, but also, distinctive site-specific variations in procurement and
technological choices”
I would remove “technological choices” from this section, as the scarcity of modified ochre
pieces does not allow to discuss technological aspects related to ochre exploitation.
Reply: Thank you for this comment. Our use of the term “technological choices” is deliberate,
and follows previous examples (MacDonald et al. 2024; Arch and Anth Sciences) that emphasize
raw material selection and procurement as a technological choice. Raw material selection is
indeed the first of several technological choices that take place along the ochre chaîne
opératoire, followed by decisions on whether to heat treat to achieve a desired hue, the
mechanical means used to turn consolidated lithic material to a powder (grinding, scoring,
pulverization), using water-based levigation or dry sieving, mixing with other inorganic or
organic materials to achieve a desired consistency or texture.
Page 4
- “communities of practice”
This concept sometimes appears in italics and sometimes not. Please be consistent.
Reply: We have corrected the manuscript text to be consistent throughout.
- “Following the local traditional nomenclature and geology of Eswatini, we use the term ochre
to describe all earth-derived mineral pigments, with specific reference to red or yellow ochre
(iron oxide and iron-rich clay), black ochre (magnetite, manganese oxides, or charcoal) and
white ochre (kaolin)”.
I understand the authors’ choice to use traditional nomenclature of Eswatini. I consider, however,
that “black ochre” and “white ochre” are slightly confusing terms, as they do not correspond to
what is usually referred to as “ochre” in the literature. The term “ochre” is already quite
ambiguous as it is, so I would recommend avoiding its use when referring to colouring materials
other than iron oxides. In any case, I see that these terms are not used throughout the text, so this
doesn’t affect the rest of the paper.
Reply: We completely agree that the term “ochre” is a broad and ambiguous term. In locally-
used language, the term is fluid depending on the context of use, but is primarily used to signify
its use as a paint, but not necessarily specific to the raw material itself. For instance, “black
ochre” is used to describe both manganese oxides or charcoal used as paint. For these reasons we
included parenthetical notes in the main text about the raw materials that could encompass those
terms, and have updated the text to convey the use of the term to specifically denote “paint”.
Page 13
- Tables 1 and 2
Some of the archaeological sites do not appear on table 1 (Mlawula I and II, Nsangwini,
Hlalakahle, Mphaphati I, Ndhlozane shelter). Are there no dates for these sites?
Reply: Regarding Table 1, you are correct – there are no radiometric dates available for each of
those sites, therefore have not been included in Table 1. In those instances, the contexts are either
very shallow and limited in cultural material (Mlawula 1), subjected to major erosion or other
secondary disturbances (Mlawula II, Hlalakahle), shallow and mixed MSA/LSA deposits
(Nsangwini), or not yet excavated and dated (e.g. surface finds from Ndhlozane shelter), At the
present time we can only infer relative or indirect temporal periods based on associations with
diagnostic tool or pottery assemblages, or in association with an ironworking kiln as seen at
Mphamphati I.
We have updated the Table 1 caption to clarify the omission of those sites.
“Table 1: List of archaeological sites and available chronometric dates included in this study.
OSL ages are shown with 1σ uncertainties. Samples studied from sites Mlawula I and II,
Nsangwini, Hlalakahle, Mphaphati I, Muti Muti, and Ndhlozane shelter lack chronometric dates

Here are brief explanations for each of the sites, quoted from information provided in
Supplementary Text.
Mlawula I and II (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.5)
Barham originally excavated the site in an L-shaped block of seven 2 m2 units and in one single
stratum as the sediment was reportedly unstratified. After excavating 10 cm deep, artifact
frequency dropped significantly and was thus declared sterile. The assemblage was characterized
by LSA artifacts mixed with Iron Age pottery. A glass bead indicates that the entire occupation

As I already stated in my first review, this paper is in my opinion an outstanding contribution to
ochre studies. By using different analytical techniques, including pXRF, NAA, LA-ICP-MS, XRD and

interest to the understanding of late MSA and LSA cultures. The authors have thoroughly taken into
account suggestions made by myself and reviewer #2. All of the data is presented in the article and
supplementary data. I have no additional comments on the paper and I strongly recommend
publication.

### Reviewer 1

This paper is in my opinion an outstanding contribution to ochre studies. The identification of an
ochre community of practice represents an innovative approach that certainly represents a
necessary step in the study of earth mineral pigments. The authors use different analytical
techniques, including pXRF, NAA, LA-ICP-MS, XRD and Raman spectroscopy to characterise raw
materials from different archaeological sites and potential sources. These methods are in line with
the questions raised and enable the authors to reconstruct patterns of raw material acquisition that
are of great interest to the understanding of late MSA and LSA cultures. All of the data is thoroughly
presented in the article and supplementary data. I strongly recommend publication.
Please find below a few minor comments and suggestions by page number:
Page 3
- “The analysis of earth mineral pigments, or ochres, has played a role in interpretations of cognitive
behaviors (6, 7), has become synonymous with rock art and symbolic expressions”
I would not say that the use of ochre is synonymous with symbolic expressions. As this is a quite
debated question, I would advise being more cautious in this statement.
- “Here, we apply the concept to the chaîne opératoire of ochre behaviors”.
Considering that the technological aspects of the ochre exploitation strategies and possible uses of
ochre are not explored in this paper, I would say that the concept of community of practice is
mostly applied here to raw material acquisition strategies, rather than the entire ochre chaîne
opératoire,
- “These components were selected (…) also for sociocultural reasons, such as spiritual potency
and the geographic origins of minerals. The ochre chaîne opératoire was an inherently social
activity that existed as part of a broader system of relations that had cultural significance to people
living in the MSA and LSA.”
I agree with this statement. However, we do not have direct evidence of it for MSA and LSA cultures.
I would advise moderating this section by specifying that it is a likely hypothesis.
- “Here, we show evidence for long term, regional-scale behavioral stability in ochre provisioning
and transport, but also, distinctive site-specific variations in procurement and technological
choices”
I would remove “technological choices” from this section, as the scarcity of modified ochre pieces
does not allow to discuss technological aspects related to ochre exploitation.
Page 4
- “communities of practice”
This concept sometimes appears in italics and sometimes not. Please be consistent.
- “Following the local traditional nomenclature and geology of Eswatini, we use the term ochre
to describe all earth-derived mineral pigments, with specific reference to red or yellow ochre (iron
oxide and iron-rich clay), black ochre (magnetite, manganese oxides, or charcoal) and
white ochre (kaolin)”.
I understand the authors’ choice to use traditional nomenclature of Eswatini. I consider, however,
that “black ochre” and “white ochre” are slightly confusing terms, as they do not correspond to
what is usually referred to as “ochre” in the literature. The term “ochre” is already quite ambiguous
as it is, so I would recommend avoiding its use when referring to colouring materials other than iron
oxides. In any case, I see that these terms are not used throughout the text, so this doesn’t affect
the rest of the paper.
Page 13
- Tables 1 and 2
Some of the archaeological sites do not appear on table 1 (Mlawula I and II, Nsangwini, Hlalakahle,
Mphaphati I, Ndhlozane shelter). Are there no dates for these sites?
Page 15
- In figure legend 2b, what do the authors mean exactly by “use wear”?
Page 16
- Figure 3 is missing
Page 17
- Figure 4 is missing.
Page 19-20
- Figure 5 and 6: I recommend specifying in the figure legend that the scatterplot represents the
PCA of NAA results.
Page 27-28
- Figures 8 and 9: adding the total number of iron and manganese artifacts per phase to the figure
might be useful to evaluate how significative these proportions are, and to have an idea of the
stratigraphic distribution of these pieces.
Page 32
- “Hunter-gatherers would have conducted some testing (grinding, scoring, mixing, applying to
various surfaces, see SI-Text 2.0) to understand their qualities for rock art or body paint,
adhesives, and other potential uses”.
I was surprised by the fact that the technological observations conducted on the archaeological
assemblage are only mentioned in the supplementary materials. I think that, although very few
pieces show modifications, this aspect deserves to appear in the main text, and maybe they could
be presented in the form of a table. Unless I’m mistaken, I don’t think there is detailed information
on the stratigraphic provenance of modified pieces (in addition to what appears in page 29 of the
Supplementary text). In the case of Sibebe, it is not specified in the supplementary data which
ochre typologies show anthropogenic modifications.
Page 33
“The infrequent long-distance transport of ochre could be indicative of the itinerant movement of
painters or tangoma (…) the localized activities associated with its chaîne opératoire were varied
and contextually-contingent communities of practice”.
While these ethnographic examples are of great interest and show the cultural significance of
ochre, I think that using this information to discuss MSA and LSA societies is a complex task. I
would suggest the authors mention the fact that there are debates surrounding ethnoarchaeology,
and on whether one should establish analogies between prehistoric societies and ethnographic
data. Maybe it would be interesting to cite some authors that have discussed this issue, such as
David and Kramer 2001 (David N, Kramer C. Ethnoarchaeology in Action. Cambridge: Cambridge
University Press; 2001.).

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This paper is in my opinion an outstanding contribution to ochre studies. The identification of an
ochre community of practice represents an innovative approach that certainly represents a
necessary step in the study of earth mineral pigments. The authors use different analytical
techniques, including pXRF, NAA, LA-ICP-MS, XRD and Raman spectroscopy to characterise raw
materials from different archaeological sites and potential sources. These methods are in line with
the questions raised and enable the authors to reconstruct patterns of raw material acquisition that
are of great interest to the understanding of late MSA and LSA cultures. All of the data is thoroughly
presented in the article and supplementary data. I strongly recommend publication.
Please find below a few minor comments and suggestions by page number:
Page 3
- “The analysis of earth mineral pigments, or ochres, has played a role in interpretations of cognitive
behaviors (6, 7), has become synonymous with rock art and symbolic expressions”
I would not say that the use of ochre is synonymous with symbolic expressions. As this is a quite
debated question, I would advise being more cautious in this statement.
- “Here, we apply the concept to the chaîne opératoire of ochre behaviors”.
Considering that the technological aspects of the ochre exploitation strategies and possible uses of
ochre are not explored in this paper, I would say that the concept of community of practice is
mostly applied here to raw material acquisition strategies, rather than the entire ochre chaîne
opératoire,
- “These components were selected (…) also for sociocultural reasons, such as spiritual potency
and the geographic origins of minerals. The ochre chaîne opératoire was an inherently social
activity that existed as part of a broader system of relations that had cultural significance to people
living in the MSA and LSA.”
I agree with this statement. However, we do not have direct evidence of it for MSA and LSA cultures.
I would advise moderating this section by specifying that it is a likely hypothesis.
- “Here, we show evidence for long term, regional-scale behavioral stability in ochre provisioning
and transport, but also, distinctive site-specific variations in procurement and technological
choices”
I would remove “technological choices” from this section, as the scarcity of modified ochre pieces
does not allow to discuss technological aspects related to ochre exploitation.
Page 4
- “communities of practice”
This concept sometimes appears in italics and sometimes not. Please be consistent.
- “Following the local traditional nomenclature and geology of Eswatini, we use the term ochre

oxide and iron-rich clay), black ochre (magnetite, manganese oxides, or charcoal) and

I understand the authors’ choice to use traditional nomenclature of Eswatini. I consider, however,

### Reviewer 2

LSA in Eswatini. The authors have sampled ochre from known archaeological sites from recent or
ancient excavations, as well as from potential ancient mining sites. A panel of physico-chemical
analyses (NAA, La-ICPMS, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, XRF) has allowed them to defined different

sceptical about the fact that part of the discussion could be derived from general considerations on
ochre use (ex: the need to share the location of sources and the way to use them) and not from

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We sincerely thank the two anonymous reviewers for their feedback and suggestions for
improvement on our manuscript. We provide our point-by-point response here in BLUE.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper is in my opinion an outstanding contribution to ochre studies. The identification of an
ochre community of practice represents an innovative approach that certainly represents a
necessary step in the study of earth mineral pigments. The authors use different analytical
techniques, including pXRF, NAA, LA-ICP-MS, XRD and Raman spectroscopy to characterise
raw materials from different archaeological sites and potential sources. These methods are in line
with the questions raised and enable the authors to reconstruct patterns of raw material
acquisition that are of great interest to the understanding of late MSA and LSA cultures. All of

publication.
Reply: Thank you for your kind words and valuable feedback on our manuscript.
Page 3
- “The analysis of earth mineral pigments, or ochres, has played a role in interpretations of
cognitive behaviors (6, 7), has become synonymous with rock art and symbolic expressions”

mostly applied here to raw material acquisition strategies, rather than the entire ochre chaîne
opératoire,

currently convey with confidence about the uses of ochre. Please note that we are constrained by

supplementary text to the main text and have added and cited a brief comparison to the
proportion of ochre usewear found at comparable sites. We also added further commentary

Ochre Processing and Use
Figure 10 illustrates a selection of ochre samples exhibiting usewear from the Sibebe
assemblage. Remarkably, only nine of the 931 (< 1%) artifacts examined this entire study
showed clear evidence of usewear, six of which were from Sibebe, and four of those limited to
the uppermost stratum at that site. The remaining modified ochres were from Siphiso (n=2) and
Nyonyane (n=1). This low proportion of modified ochre artifacts in the Eswatini assemblages is
in contrast to the few other comparable systematic studies on ochre processing. For instance,
Hodgskiss’ analysis of MSA ochre at Sibudu (52) identified 7.57% of the total assemblage
exhibited evidence for usewear (more commonly during the pre-Still Bay period ~77kya), and
Hodgskiss and Wadley identified usewear (grinding, scoring, rubbing) in 11.2% of the
assemblage at Rose Cottage Cave (53). The results from the Eswatini assemblage suggests that
the more common method for preparing ochres for use as paint to for objects, rock walls, or as
body paint, may have been through grinding or pulverizing whole pieces using an anvil or
mortar and pestle, rather than via repeated abrasion or scoring of the ochre pieces against other
textured surfaces to produce powder.
Other indicators for the processing and end-use of ochre are evident in the abundance of
rock art. There are currently 52 documented (yet unpublished) rock art sites across Eswatini,
several of them coincident with the assemblages studied here (Nsangwini, Sibebe, Muti Muti,
Ndhlozane). The artifact assemblage recovered from Nsangwini also yielded 17 lithics (chert,
hornfels) stained with dry-rubbed ochre or spatters of prepared ochre paint. Further study of
those stone tools is currently underway.
- “These components were selected (…) also for sociocultural reasons, such as spiritual potency
and the geographic origins of minerals. The ochre chaîne opératoire was an inherently social
activity that existed as part of a broader system of relations that had cultural significance to
people living in the MSA and LSA.”
I agree with this statement. However, we do not have direct evidence of it for MSA and LSA
cultures. I would advise moderating this section by specifying that it is a likely hypothesis.

passage.
- “Here, we show evidence for long term, regional-scale behavioral stability in ochre
provisioning and transport, but also, distinctive site-specific variations in procurement and
technological choices”
I would remove “technological choices” from this section, as the scarcity of modified ochre
pieces does not allow to discuss technological aspects related to ochre exploitation.

and follows previous examples (MacDonald et al. 2024; Arch and Anth Sciences) that emphasize
raw material selection and procurement as a technological choice. Raw material selection is
indeed the first of several technological choices that take place along the ochre chaîne
opératoire, followed by decisions on whether to heat treat to achieve a desired hue, the
mechanical means used to turn consolidated lithic material to a powder (grinding, scoring,
pulverization), using water-based levigation or dry sieving, mixing with other inorganic or
organic materials to achieve a desired consistency or texture.
Page 4
- “communities of practice”
This concept sometimes appears in italics and sometimes not. Please be consistent.
Reply: We have corrected the manuscript text to be consistent throughout.
- “Following the local traditional nomenclature and geology of Eswatini, we use the term ochre
to describe all earth-derived mineral pigments, with specific reference to red or yellow ochre
(iron oxide and iron-rich clay), black ochre (magnetite, manganese oxides, or charcoal) and
white ochre (kaolin)”.
I understand the authors’ choice to use traditional nomenclature of Eswatini. I consider, however,
that “black ochre” and “white ochre” are slightly confusing terms, as they do not correspond to
what is usually referred to as “ochre” in the literature. The term “ochre” is already quite
ambiguous as it is, so I would recommend avoiding its use when referring to colouring materials
other than iron oxides. In any case, I see that these terms are not used throughout the text, so this
doesn’t affect the rest of the paper.
Reply: We completely agree that the term “ochre” is a broad and ambiguous term. In locally-
used language, the term is fluid depending on the context of use, but is primarily used to signify
its use as a paint, but not necessarily specific to the raw material itself. For instance, “black
ochre” is used to describe both manganese oxides or charcoal used as paint. For these reasons we
included parenthetical notes in the main text about the raw materials that could encompass those
terms, and have updated the text to convey the use of the term to specifically denote “paint”.
Page 13
- Tables 1 and 2
Some of the archaeological sites do not appear on table 1 (Mlawula I and II, Nsangwini,
Hlalakahle, Mphaphati I, Ndhlozane shelter). Are there no dates for these sites?
Reply: Regarding Table 1, you are correct – there are no radiometric dates available for each of
those sites, therefore have not been included in Table 1. In those instances, the contexts are either
very shallow and limited in cultural material (Mlawula 1), subjected to major erosion or other
secondary disturbances (Mlawula II, Hlalakahle), shallow and mixed MSA/LSA deposits
(Nsangwini), or not yet excavated and dated (e.g. surface finds from Ndhlozane shelter), At the
present time we can only infer relative or indirect temporal periods based on associations with
diagnostic tool or pottery assemblages, or in association with an ironworking kiln as seen at
Mphamphati I.
We have updated the Table 1 caption to clarify the omission of those sites.
“Table 1: List of archaeological sites and available chronometric dates included in this study.
OSL ages are shown with 1σ uncertainties. Samples studied from sites Mlawula I and II,
Nsangwini, Hlalakahle, Mphaphati I, Muti Muti, and Ndhlozane shelter lack chronometric dates
due to various site-specific contexts, detailed in Table 2 (extended data) and Supplementary Text
section 2.”
Here are brief explanations for each of the sites, quoted from information provided in
Supplementary Text.
Mlawula I and II (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.5)
Barham originally excavated the site in an L-shaped block of seven 2 m2 units and in one single
stratum as the sediment was reportedly unstratified. After excavating 10 cm deep, artifact
frequency dropped significantly and was thus declared sterile. The assemblage was characterized
by LSA artifacts mixed with Iron Age pottery. A glass bead indicates that the entire occupation
at Mlawula I is likely to be younger than 1000 AD. Mlawula II is located on a terrace some 10 m
above the Siphiso River. Barham reported that ca. 50% of the original site is likely destroyed due
to terrace erosion, leaving a truncated scatter of artifacts. The remaining site area was excavated
in seven 2 m2 units in two strata, and to a final depth of 30 cm.
Nsangwini (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.3)
The site also has an archaeological sequence, excavated by both Beaumont in 1966, and again by
Price Williams in 1978. Beaumont excavated ca. 7 m² in front of the shelter and reached a
maximum depth of 30 inches (76.2 cm). In his field notes, he refers to the presence of Iron Age,
LSA and MSA artifacts. There is comparably less information regarding the Price Williams
excavation – the only information we have is from the old find tags from the excavation
collection. The excavated sequence yielded a surface layer, a mixed MSA/LSA assemblage
below, and an MSA assemblage at the base deposit. No 14C ages were pursued. Based on our
initial screening of the material, the MSA assemblage contains several bifacial points made from
various raw materials. This could suggest that the assemblage, like Sibebe, belongs to a late stage
of the MSA. For this ochre provenance study, we selected the only three ochre artifacts available
for provenance analysis; one a surface find and the other two from the mixed MSA/LSA layer.
Hlalakahle (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.6)
Hlalakahle was one of the first sites excavated by David Price Williams in 1977. It is situated
above the Komati river banks overlooking the modern Maguga Dam. Deposits of 1-2 m
thickness are surrounded by big boulders. According to Price Williams’ interpretation,
Hlalakahle is a collapsed rock shelter, although this could never be confirmed. The majority of
the artifact-bearing deposits were found outside the boulder formation in a recent road cut. Price
Williams excavated no less than 5 m² of the site and interpreted the entire assemblage as a
palimpsest of secondary dislocated sediments. No radiocarbon ages exist for the site. The lithic
assemblage recovered and stored in the Eswatini National Museum in Lobamba is large and
indicates an exclusively MSA occupation. Big blades and points, several of them knapped from
different chert varieties are characteristic.
Ndhlozane shelter (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.8)
Ndhlozane Shelter is located in the south west of the country near the Ndhlozane Gorge. The
shelter contains several well-preserved examples of rock art on the backwalls. No excavations
have been carried out at the site, although deposits are potentially deep. Surface finds include
stone artifacts, pottery and ochre indicating at least an occupation during the Later Stone Age
and Iron Age. Six ochre artifact surface finds from Ndhlozane are included in the provenance
study presented here.
Mphatiphati I (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.9)
This Iron Age site was originally excavated by Ohinata, who studied the settlement patterns and
material culture of sites bearing ceramic and metallurgical kilns. This site was included in this
study because its excavation yielded several pieces of unprocessed ochre raw materials in
association with several dozen nodules of raw ore in association with a metallurgical kiln.
Considering this association, we inferred that the ochre raw materials from this site represent a
known locally available source of iron ore material from the Mahalamanti Valley.
Page 15
- In figure legend 2b, what do the authors mean exactly by “use wear”?
Reply: We have clarified our description of usewear in the figure caption. The term usewear
refers to any evidence for anthropogenic modification of the ochres resulting from processing,
such as grinding or scoring.
“Figure 2a (upper) Selected hand specimens of samples from sources included in this study.
Figure 2b. (lower) Examples of modified ochre artifacts from Sibebe, showing evidence for
modification, including grooves created during grinding or scoring.”

- Figure 3 is missing

- Figure 4 is missing.

Page 27-28

might be useful to evaluate how significative these proportions are, and to have an idea of the

Reply: Thank you for your comment. We are unable to embed a table within the figures due to
print specifications, but the information you seek can be found in Table 2 [Extended Data],
which, if published, be readily viewable online alongside Figures 8 and 9.
Page 32
- “Hunter-gatherers would have conducted some testing (grinding, scoring, mixing, applying to
various surfaces, see SI-Text 2.0) to understand their qualities for rock art or body paint,
adhesives, and other potential uses”.
I was surprised by the fact that the technological observations conducted on the archaeological
assemblage are only mentioned in the supplementary materials. I think that, although very few
pieces show modifications, this aspect deserves to appear in the main text, and maybe they could
be presented in the form of a table. Unless I’m mistaken, I don’t think there is detailed
information on the stratigraphic provenance of modified pieces (in addition to what appears in
page 29 of the Supplementary text). In the case of Sibebe, it is not specified in the supplementary
data which ochre typologies show anthropogenic modifications.
Reply: We moved the discussion of the observations on modifications and usewear to the main
text. We added text on the types that had evident usewear (specularite and fine-grained
consolidated hematite, Types 2 and 1c). In all instances, the finds are restricted to LSA deposits.
Page 33
“The infrequent long-distance transport of ochre could be indicative of the itinerant movement of
painters or tangoma (…) the localized activities associated with its chaîne opératoire were varied
and contextually-contingent communities of practice”.
While these ethnographic examples are of great interest and show the cultural significance of
ochre, I think that using this information to discuss MSA and LSA societies is a complex task. I
would suggest the authors mention the fact that there are debates surrounding ethnoarchaeology,
and on whether one should establish analogies between prehistoric societies and ethnographic
data. Maybe it would be interesting to cite some authors that have discussed this issue, such as
David and Kramer 2001 (David N, Kramer C. Ethnoarchaeology in Action. Cambridge:
Cambridge University Press; 2001.).
Reply: We agree. While ethnographic analogy cannot and does not explain the past, it is a useful
tool for expanding our understanding of possible drivers of human behaviours and decision-
making. We have added this clarification to the text.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
LSA in Eswatini. The authors have sampled ochre from known archaeological sites from recent
or ancient excavations, as well as from potential ancient mining sites. A panel of physico-
chemical analyses (NAA, La-ICPMS, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, XRF) has allowed them to
defined different groups of ochre (Mn or Fe rich types) and to propose sourcing for the
archaeological samples. Then discussions about procurement strategies over time are presented.
The paper is overall well written and structured with a very complete set of data and documents.
I am not competent to judge the way in which the statistical study was carried out. I am also a bit
sceptical about the fact that part of the discussion could be derived from general considerations
on ochre use (ex: the need to share the location of sources and the way to use them) and not from
the data presented and analysed here. This should not prevent the paper to be published however.
I have only minor suggestions and comments:
- I think a summary map (or several) showing relations between archaeological sites and mining
sources deduced from the analyses would be useful. I add to draw arrows on the map in order to
follow the conclusions, so it might be good if this was already provided by the authors.

movement. Finally, there are so many sources and sites included in this study that adding more

produce with the information in hand. Please bear in mind that no locational information is
currently available for sources G2b, G2c, G2d, G3, G4, MnG2, MnG3, and MnG6.

Figure: Origin and deposition of Bulembu ochre (G1b) and manganese oxide (MnG1).

Figure: Origin and deposition of Mahalamanti Valley ochre (G5).

this context and instead referred to the “extracted ochres and their properties for intended use”,

properties for their intended use, among which would have included colorfastness, impurities,

weathering, and adhesion to a surface.”

strength of the material”-> “led to reduce”

sites is forms might be different from the way in which any living sites builds up.

SI Figure 25: Profile view of Lion Cavern showing the distribution of archaeological deposits,

in iron. Did you consider this in your calculations of dose rate? How different would be the
absorption coefficients?

Reply: Yes, we used the a-value system. We have added this information to the supplementary
material. We furthermore added the following sentence to the supplementary section outlining
details of the performed age calculations.
“To account for the different efficiencies in producing luminescence of alpha-particles,
compared to beta and gamma radiation, the a-value determined for our samples (0.042 ± 0.005)

not very explicit about the process and Table 6 presents the data only for the OSL samples. How
many samples did you use to reconstruct the gamma dose? How did you deal with
heterogeneities if any?
Reply: Thank you for your comment. We added the following sentence to supplementary section
6.1:
“Due to the homogeneity of the surrounding sediment, one dosimetry sample per OSL sample
was taken and used for external dose rate calculations for each OSL sample, respectively.”
We also modified the section regarding “dose rate determination” slightly, to accommodate more
information.
- In Table 6: I guess the K content is actually in %, not in ppm. Please also indicate that the DR
is in Gy/ka. I think the second digit is not significant for the De, nor for the Age. Please remove
them. This is also the case in Table 1 in the main text.
Reply: Thank you very much for pointing out the error in the units used for K. It should be %
and not ppm. We changed this accordingly. We also added the units for the cosmic and
environmental dose rates. Furthermore, we rounded the values given for doses and ages.

by LSA artifacts mixed with Iron Age pottery. A glass bead indicates that the entire occupation
at Mlawula I is likely to be younger than 1000 AD. Mlawula II is located on a terrace some 10 m
above the Siphiso River. Barham reported that ca. 50% of the original site is likely destroyed due
to terrace erosion, leaving a truncated scatter of artifacts. The remaining site area was excavated
in seven 2 m2 units in two strata, and to a final depth of 30 cm.
Nsangwini (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.3)
The site also has an archaeological sequence, excavated by both Beaumont in 1966, and again by
Price Williams in 1978. Beaumont excavated ca. 7 m² in front of the shelter and reached a
maximum depth of 30 inches (76.2 cm). In his field notes, he refers to the presence of Iron Age,
LSA and MSA artifacts. There is comparably less information regarding the Price Williams
excavation – the only information we have is from the old find tags from the excavation
collection. The excavated sequence yielded a surface layer, a mixed MSA/LSA assemblage
below, and an MSA assemblage at the base deposit. No 14C ages were pursued. Based on our
initial screening of the material, the MSA assemblage contains several bifacial points made from
various raw materials. This could suggest that the assemblage, like Sibebe, belongs to a late stage
of the MSA. For this ochre provenance study, we selected the only three ochre artifacts available
for provenance analysis; one a surface find and the other two from the mixed MSA/LSA layer.
Hlalakahle (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.6)
Hlalakahle was one of the first sites excavated by David Price Williams in 1977. It is situated
above the Komati river banks overlooking the modern Maguga Dam. Deposits of 1-2 m
thickness are surrounded by big boulders. According to Price Williams’ interpretation,
Hlalakahle is a collapsed rock shelter, although this could never be confirmed. The majority of
the artifact-bearing deposits were found outside the boulder formation in a recent road cut. Price
Williams excavated no less than 5 m² of the site and interpreted the entire assemblage as a
palimpsest of secondary dislocated sediments. No radiocarbon ages exist for the site. The lithic
assemblage recovered and stored in the Eswatini National Museum in Lobamba is large and
indicates an exclusively MSA occupation. Big blades and points, several of them knapped from
different chert varieties are characteristic.
Ndhlozane shelter (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.8)
Ndhlozane Shelter is located in the south west of the country near the Ndhlozane Gorge. The
shelter contains several well-preserved examples of rock art on the backwalls. No excavations
have been carried out at the site, although deposits are potentially deep. Surface finds include
stone artifacts, pottery and ochre indicating at least an occupation during the Later Stone Age
and Iron Age. Six ochre artifact surface finds from Ndhlozane are included in the provenance
study presented here.
Mphatiphati I (quoted from Supplementary Text section 2.9)
This Iron Age site was originally excavated by Ohinata, who studied the settlement patterns and
material culture of sites bearing ceramic and metallurgical kilns. This site was included in this
study because its excavation yielded several pieces of unprocessed ochre raw materials in
association with several dozen nodules of raw ore in association with a metallurgical kiln.
Considering this association, we inferred that the ochre raw materials from this site represent a
known locally available source of iron ore material from the Mahalamanti Valley.
